Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the automaker noted Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.
  • The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

According to recent reports, the automaker noted Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

Industry observers note that the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Sources indicate that alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, stated licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

It has been revealed that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Industry observers note that in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial prepares of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford mentioned it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • State to execute man convicted of two counts of first-degree murder while Texas also aims to put a man to death.
  • Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist.
  • In a recent development, thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6pm at Florida state prison in Raiford.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

State to execute man convicted of two counts of first-degree murder while Texas also aims to put a man to death.

Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist.

In a recent development, thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6pm at Florida state prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, was set to receive a lethal injection about an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the ageing of the US death row population.

Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office in January 1996.

Industry observers note that on Thursday, Overton woke up at 5am and remained compliant, a Florida department of corrections spokesperson, Jordan Kirkland, noted during a news conference. He did not meet with any visitors or a spiritual adviser.

According to recent reports, florida has carried out more than half the nation’s 37 executions this year under Ron DeSantis, the state’s outgoing Republican governor who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday’s scheduled executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US after Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in October.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

On Thursday, the US supreme court denied a final appeal in the Florida case while an appeal remained pending in the Texas case.

Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence.

The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home in August 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Recent findings suggest that investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene but initially found no match with samples in the state’s database. But Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities stated a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors’ home, and he was charged with their killings.

Recent findings suggest that in the Texas case, Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’s request.

The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his attacker.

Recent findings suggest that police found the jeweler’s body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents remarked officers found the jeweler’s safe empty with no sign of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand. The diamonds have never been recovered.

Dennes’s attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs.

Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022.

“I did those things, so I am guilty,” Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor’s filing stated.

It has been revealed that A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

Tech Report: Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure and end Rheinmetall deal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.
  • The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season.
  • "It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.

The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season. Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer confirmed the news on the club's website ahead of its AGM on Sunday, which may have proved a potential flashpoint. He acknowledged that "our partnership has been controversial from the outset" but lamented the loss of income.

"It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre. We will have to reprioritize planned investments and carefully examine how we can find viable solutions.".

Though he welcomed the news, one of the leaders of the fan revolt against the partnership, Michael Schulze von Glaser, warned this is likely not the end of the road.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"I think in the end it was a victory for the fans. But I'm also a bit skeptical about  what the future will bring us," the Dortmund fan and former head of the German Peace Society told DW. "Football fans in Germany always must be skeptical and always must watch what the club is doing.”.

It has been revealed that many Dortmund fans have opposed the deal — which has seen Rheinmetall's logo on advertising boards and other surfaces at locations such as Dortmund's 83,000-capacity Westfalenstadion — from its beginnings in 2024. It was estimated to be worth between €7 ($7.68 million) and €9 million per year.

At the club's AGM that year, 556 of 855 members present voted against the deal in a non-binding vote. There were 247 votes in favour, with 52 abstentions. This, said Cramer, informed the eventual outcome.

Rheinmetall sells arms mostly to Germany, Ukraine and NATO but fans and critics feel that platforming any arms manufacturer goes against the club's statement of its core values. In that, Dortmund states its desire for "a club and a society that operate free of racism, anti-Semitism, LGBTQIA+ hostility, sexism, violence and discrimination.".

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio.

It has always been clear, said Schulze von Glaser, that this deal did not chime with that.

"In the end, they kill people. They are for war," he said of Rheinmetall. "The slogan of Borussia Dortmund is true love (Echte Liebe). But for me and many others, our love ends there…. I know some fans who have put fan merchandise in the trash because they were so shocked.”.

According to recent reports, in the Q and A on the club's website, Cramer mentioned he was still a "personal advocate" of the deal but that Dortmund's commitment to the 50+1 model, which means German clubs are majority controlled by the members, meant they had to listen to fan voices. But he also warned that Rheinmetall must be an "absolute exception and an isolated case.".

That set off some alarm bells for Schulze von Glaser.

"It's a bit concerning that there are constantly these attacks on professional football — a latest sponsorship, investment deals," he stated.

In a recent development, indeed, Dortmund's climbdown is not the first of its kind in Germany's top flight. Last year, after fan and media pressure, Bayern Munich ended its commercial deal with the tourism arm of the Rwandan government before its conclusion.

Fans had objected to the promotion of Rwanda, which many felt sought to divert attention from its poor human rights record and actions in the war with DR Congo, through sporting partnerships. Two years earlier, Bayern withdrew from a similarly controversial deal with Qatar Airways.

In a recent development, elsewhere in the league, Werder Bremen fans objected to their long time shirt sponsor, Wiesenhof. Many supporters took concern with the factory farming practices  of Germany's largest poultry producer. Though it was not given as a direct reason for the end of a shirt sponsorship deal in 2023, it likely played a part.

Union Berlin fans have also made their voices heard. When the club signed a new shirt-sponsorship deal with Luxembourg real estate tech giant, Aroundtown, upon promotion to the top flight in 2019, many fans were frustrated at the tie up in a city where rent prices were skyrocketing.

"It's a problem for a lot of people," fan Sven Dobberstein told DW at the time.

Industry observers note that "We have to try to find a way between commercialization and what we have at the moment. It isn't easy.".

Industry observers note that striking that balance can often be a source of tension for Bundesliga clubs. 50+1 ensures fans have a voice, preventing rich owners, or nation states, from taking control as they do in England's lucrative Premier League or in France or Spain. Indeed fan protests have also stopped the league signing a €1billion private equity partner and seen Monday night matches scrapped. For Schulze von Glaser, this needs to be protected.

"In Germany, the fan culture has an impact," he mentioned.

”If there is something bad or terrible happening in your club and in the Bundesliga, there are the organized fans and they can have an impact if they want, if they stand together and, yes, they can stop the Rheinmetall deal.".

Additional reporting by: Emmie Eernisse.

The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Sources indicate that hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s so much more than the four names that have been confirmed,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

Sources indicate that glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

Industry observers note that the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

According to recent reports, if all goes to blueprint, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton said via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already noted delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

It has been revealed that the space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

It has been revealed that vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

“I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche remarked. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

Sources indicate that “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She said the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

In a recent development, “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

Anime has never been bigger, and if you have been meaning to catch up on fall simulcasts or plow through a backlog of classics, Crunchyroll just kicked off a rare Black Friday sale that makes signing up a whole lot cheaper.

Unlike streaming promos that only discount the cheapest base tier, Crunchyroll has slashed U.S. prices across all three of its membership levels — Fan, Mega Fan, and Ultimate Fan.

Normally $9.99 per month, the entry-level Fan tier drops to $3.99 per month for your first six months — saving you $6 every month, or $36 total.

It covers all the essentials if you are only watching for yourself: ad-free streaming across Crunchyroll's anime library (note that looks may still include brief trailers or promotional messages before playback), new episodes shortly after they air in Japan, HD downloads for offline viewing, and streaming on 1 device at a time.

If you share an account or want extra gaming and shopping perks, Mega Fan drops from its usual $13.99 per month down to $5.99 per month for six months — saving you $8 a month, or $48 over the promo period.

Mega Fan includes everything in the Fan tier, bumps simultaneous streaming up to 4 devices at once, and unlocks access to Crunchyroll Game Vault (a library of 100+ mobile games with no ads or in-app purchases) besides access to exclusive Crunchyroll Store drops and free U.S. shipping on orders of $50 or more.

Crunchyroll's top-tier Ultimate Fan plan is also cut in half for six months, dropping from $17.99 per month to $8.99 per month — saving you $9 each month, or $54 total.

Along with everything in Mega Fan, Ultimate Fan lets you stream on up to 6 devices at the same time, unlocks Crunchyroll Manga access in select countries (with ad-free reading on iOS, Android, and crunchyroll.com/manga for series like The Apothecary Diaries, My Dress-Up Darling, and Re:ZERO -Starting Life in Another World-, which Mega Fan members can also add separately), gives you free shipping on all Crunchyroll Store orders with no minimum, grants early access to drops, and includes an exclusive swag bag after 12 consecutive months of membership.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical challenges behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

It has been revealed that the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a latest router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris remarked that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators noted within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Politicians call attack on independent councillor Ibrar Ali canvassing in Bradford Moor ward ‘deeply disturbing’.

Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.

West Yorkshire police said there was nothing to suggest the incident was politically motivated, although the investigation was at an early stage.

Jim McMahon, the MP for Oldham West, described the attack as “horrific” and stated: “Our thoughts are with [Ali], his family, councillors in Bradford and, of course, our members of parliament too.

“Our thoughts are very much with you all at this time.”.

Recent findings suggest that imran Hussain, the MP for Bradford East, stated: “This horrific attack is deeply disturbing. My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family.

In a recent development, “No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community. I am receiving regular updates from the police as they deal with this extremely serious incident, and I understand a suspect is in police custody.”.

Officers were called just after 11am to reports that a 52-year-old man, a serving Bradford councillor, had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

It has been revealed that police noted: “The man is believed to have first been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to Manse Street where emergency services attended. He was taken to hospital where his condition is described as serious but not life-threatening.”.

A 32-year-old man fled to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue but was brought down some time later and arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, named Ali in the House of Lords. Lady Taylor mentioned: “I am afraid I have to mention a very tragic incident that’s occurred in Bradford … where an independent councillor who was out canvassing has been stabbed.

“I would want to send the wishes, that I’m sure noble lords would agree, of the whole house to councillor Ibrar Ali for a speedy recovery, and our thoughts are with all of those in Bradford who are affected by this awful incident.”.

Police cordons were in place on Manse Street, Leeds Road and Thornbury Avenue while inquiries are carried out.

Recent findings suggest that adam, who works in the area and did not want to give his surname, mentioned: “I know the councillor on a personal level and it’s shocking. I just know he’s a very kind, warm-hearted man whose goal is to serve, his life is to help out everyone.

Sources indicate that “He just wants everyone to succeed. He definitely didn’t deserve what’s happened.

“The world’s not a nice place.”.

Chris Herd, the lord mayor of Bradford, said: “It is deeply distressing that this incident has occurred.

“Councillors work tirelessly on behalf of residents across the district and should be able to carry out their duties safely.

“We will continue to work closely with our colleagues at West Yorkshire police as they investigate this matter and seek to bring those responsible to justice, and would like to thank those who provided aid and support at the time.”.

Press Association contributed to this report.

Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.
  • The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.
  • The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

Industry observers note that in the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick stated Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

According to recent reports, "If you get to a firm with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued.".

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

Recent findings suggest that "Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation firm," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money.".

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction.".

Industry observers note that "We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie.".

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

Industry observers note that with many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

It has been revealed that "They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs.".

In a recent development, that has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to problem upcoming AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have confirmed deals worth $67 billion.

Rees remarked another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that in his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

Sources indicate that when the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’.
  • The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.
  • After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’.

The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.

After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.

A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed.

Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.

“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”.

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.

It has been revealed that it is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.

Recent reports have claimed that Brand, who is jailed in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, is likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead after protesting his innocence.

It is understood that there has been no such proposal, and he is likely to remain in Littlehey, a specialist prison for sex offenders.

The government has no power to compel YouTube’s direct owner, Google, to remove the video, but has been in “dialogue” with the tech firm over it.

“We trust that they will do the right thing,” a Downing Street spokesperson mentioned when asked about the standoff. They said: “The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.

According to recent reports, “We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.”.

Recent findings suggest that no 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: “Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.”.

A spokesperson for Google said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”.

Kemi Badenoch stated if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.

According to recent reports, the Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.

“I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart remarked global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

In a recent development, walmart mentioned it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the manufacturer has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey stated Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

According to recent reports, for the quarter ended Oct. 31, the organization reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Recent findings suggest that furner also remarked Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he mentioned.

It has been revealed that sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It remarked its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

It has been revealed that in October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

It has been revealed that furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the tech giant reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The tech giant on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

Sources indicate that the tech giant is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

In a recent development, the major-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic.
  • In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
  • The organization behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic.

In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The organization behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it remarked on Wednesday.

At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (Â£14.7bn) each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it released Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

It has been revealed that initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile.

In a recent development, dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she claims, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their newly introduced venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the manufacturer secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

According to recent reports, now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

In a recent development, jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.

Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.

But according to the Fresh York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.

Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.

He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.

The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sources indicate that sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

Henry Nicholls made an unbeaten 113 to help New Zealand recover from 70-5 to finish the first day of the first Test at 243-5 in Wellington on Thursday. India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and chose to bowl.

Jasprit Bumrah, playing his first Test in about a year, bowled Fresh Zealand captain Tom Latham with the third ball of the match. He finished with 3-52 from 17 overs, adding Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell.

Nicholls and Glenn Phillips then added an unbroken 173 after lunch as the pitch eased and India's other pacers lost their lines. Nicholls' 12th Test hundred came from 188 balls, 141 of them dot balls.

It has been revealed that devdutt Padikkal dropped him on 102. Phillips was 94 not out.

Parts of Bangladesh shut down Thursday as police reported two members of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed and the ancestral home of former interim leader Muhammad Yunus was set on fire.

The unrest comes ahead of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's planned return from exile in India next month, despite facing the death sentence there.

Her party, the Awami League, which was banned after Hasina was ousted, called for the nationwide "lockdown" after a week of protests over the government's rejection of her request for a new passport and identity card.

Sources indicate that police said two local BNP leaders were killed in Narail when Awami League activists attacked a BNP march, local media reported. It added that two other people, a local BNP leader and a transport worker, died in Faridpur and Pirojpur earlier this week.

Newspaper reports mentioned suspected BNP activists attacked or set fire to the homes of two Awami League leaders in Dhaka.

Crude bombs went off in Dhaka before dawn and at least four people were wounded, the Press Trust of India reported. Reuters remarked 97 platoons of the Border Guard had been deployed across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur.

Authorities mentioned flammable material was probably thrown into an unused ground-floor room of Yunus's Chattogram family home, and that relatives living upstairs were safe. At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices, which Yunus founded, have been targeted since November 10, the bank said.

Odisha has evacuated tens of thousands of people ahead of Cyclone Akvan, which is expected to cross the coast by noon Friday, the third severe cyclonic storm to threaten India's east coast in less than a month.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) expects landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha with winds up to 110 kmph. The IMD now expects a severe cyclonic storm, not the very severe storm it projected earlier. Local media reported red alerts for heavy to extremely heavy rain in both states.

Reuters cited the chief minister's office, which stated more than 47,000 people had been evacuated by Thursday. Local media put the figure at about 50,000 and said 3,000 cyclone shelters had been opened.

Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi said most evacuees were from Ganjam district. Schools in Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal are shut for three days from Thursday. Later, authorities announced that schools in Malkangiri, Rayagada and Koraput districts would also remain closed on Thursday and Friday.

It has been revealed that "No evacuations in Andhra Pradesh yet," state disaster official Prakhar Jain told Reuters. "The storm has reduced in intensity.".

Cyclone Arnab struck the region in late October and Cyclone Murasu earlier this month.

They love to be outdoors, sip craft beer, and of course, wear Patagonia fleece sweaters.

Outdoorsy folk have taken to TikTok with the hashtags #granolagirl, #granolaboy, and #granolacheck over the last few years to show off their adventurous, outdoor-oriented lifestyles. For many, getting into nature was a direct response to feeling cooped up during the lockdowns of the early pandemic. But that trend is here to stay.

For people who are unsure about adventure gear themselves but still want to find the perfect granola gift this holiday season, we chatted with outdoor expert and REI soft goods Lead and Virtual Outfitter Mike Kreis for some outdoor gear shopping tips.

Sources indicate that kreis suggests that you consider how long your giftee has been into their activity, whether it's hiking, skiing, camping, or climbing. "The longer they have been doing the activity, the more gear they will have," he states.

Industry observers note that if your gift recipient already owns some gear, Kreis notes it's best to go for nonessentials. "I always like to go with items that aren't necessarily needed for the activity, as they most likely have that," he says. So opt for a portable charger, a cozy outdoor blanket, or extra camp cooking gadgets. Really, anything that can make outdoor life more comfortable will make a great gift.

Industry observers note that if you find yourself shopping for the outdoorsy person in your life, look no further. We've rounded up 30 of the best presents out there, whether their version of adventure is having a picnic in the park or roughing it in the back country.

#47272. Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1355 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet.
  • Sources indicate that some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the firm’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before.
  • It has been revealed that the case for pessimism over the long term rests on complications that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models.

Sources indicate that some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the firm’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Anthropic shares, trading under the ticker symbol ANT, jumped more than 30 percent when they debuted on Nasdaq midday Thursday.

It has been revealed that the case for pessimism over the long term rests on complications that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models.

“The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” notes Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?”.

Sources indicate that then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the manufacturer could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth.

It has been revealed that the San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the organization held back a upcoming model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates.

Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI development. It also represents a triumph for the handful of renegade engineers and business leaders who started it. They siphoned themselves off from OpenAI in the midst of the pandemic nearly six years ago over strategic differences, and the two companies have been rivals ever since.

For some time, OpenAI was expected to go public first, but executive departures, shifting priorities, and legal troubles have introduced roadblocks.

Anthropic also has some compelling numbers to show investors. Revenue is soaring, while operating losses are declining. Its major spat with the US Department of Defense this year over limits on Claude use doesn’t appear to have significantly slowed growth. Overall, the number of customers spending six figures annually is up 12 times compared to a year ago. “I don’t think you could have dreamt of an [IPO prospectus] that’s as good,” says Tomasz Tunguz, general partner at the investment firm Theory Ventures.

Because of how Anthropic must account for compensating employees with stock, it’s still wildly unprofitable—over $104 billion in losses this year through September. That’s no matter when investors are eager to buy shares and lend money.

The IPO raised about $81 billion (more than $107 billion when adding in private sales of shares), which is more than the $75 billion SpaceX received in June in a previous world record. Anthropic’s initial valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion fell short of SpaceX’s nearly $1.8 trillion, though the Elon Musk-led rocket maker does have a more sprawling business beyond AI. (OpenAI has been valued at $1.25 trillion in an ongoing fundraising campaign.).

According to recent reports, anthropic reportedly sought, but failed, to achieve a higher valuation, suggesting some anxiety on Wall Street. US midterm election results have increased the possibility of newly introduced regulations on emerging technologies. Fears about the debt enabling AI data center development are rising, and a potential pullback in investment from Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden exit are deepening those worries.

Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have insisted investors are bullish in the long term because demand for AI models is surging. But it’s questionable whether the companies can sustain their business without coming up with ever more powerful models that drive their profits by enabling customers to automate newly introduced types of work. Without eye-catching capabilities, customers could shift to cheaper alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that some Anthropic employees have taken the safety concerns to extremes. Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic in September, citing a belief that humanity could be destroyed within a couple of years without even more focus on keeping models under human control. But, more recently, Coxon was quoted by the Stanford Daily as saying that he might return to Anthropic because he suspects he could have “more of an impact” working on safety there.

Notably, Amodei mentioned safety as a challenge even above access to electricity for data centers, which many other AI companies list as their top glitch. On the ground, people opposing data centers have griped about not just higher power bills, but also construction-induced traffic and housing woes, environmental pollution, and a lack of significant financial benefit.

It has been revealed that at data center developer Nscale’s site for Anthropic in West Virginia, extreme rain combined with grading (leveling or sloping ground for construction) coincided with flooding in neighbor’s backyards. “We’re frustrated, we’re angry,” the community spokesperson Matheny says. “We want [data centers] in more logical locations and not to be considering profit as the only guideline.” (Nscale says it has fixed damage and bought out some homeowners at above-market rates.).

Environmental activists have pointed out that Anthropic has made no commitment about using renewable power at its data centers, and has never published an environmental impact report.

It has been revealed that “Clearly permitting a fresh data center development will be extremely difficult in the US,” Tunguz indicates. Pushback could force Anthropic and others to focus outside the US for data centers. That will add risk, complexity, and cost, he says.

A handful of labor groups and others including National Nurses United urged retirement funds to steer clear of the IPO, saying they “should not be invested in companies that harm our communities and allow a handful of individuals to accumulate historic fortunes and power.”.

Industry observers note that yolanda Daniel, a member of the homeowner associations’ coalition Environmental Advocates Mississippi, states Anthropic is socializing the cost of AI development and privatizing the gains from it. “That is not how a public benefit corporation operates,” she says, vowing to do everything she can to stop next year’s planned opening of an Anthropic data center across the street from her.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s IPO paperwork argued some of its public benefit will materialize as employees and early investors become some of the world’s biggest philanthropists. But there’s no guarantee of that, or that anyone will give away their money to causes that directly benefit disgruntled communities. And if employees donate shares to one of the philanthropic funds the tech giant offers, they also consolidate power with Amodei by handing over their voting rights to him.

In a recent development, amodei and his fellow cofounders collectively hold a majority of Anthropic’s shareholder voting power. Some investor watchdogs have warned about what they view as concentrated control. But a successful debut has shown investors are entrusting Amodei and his associates with building the biggest organization in the world—that is if he can find the employees and data centers to do it.

  • Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actors Mark Lewis Jones and Osian Morgan, who voiced characters in dub of 1977 film, among guests on red carpet.

It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise.

Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening.

Among those on the red carpet was Mark Lewis Jones, who has appeared in shows ranging from The Crown to Game of Thrones and had a role in the 2017 Star Wars film The Last Jedi. In this version of Star Wars, he is a Welsh Darth Vader.

He mentioned he thought Welsh was a good language for Vader. “It has an ancient, poetic sense. It gives him that status, that authority,” said Jones, who hails from the Wrexham area in north-east Wales. “I give all my characters north-east Wales accents,” he said.

Also taking a bow was Osian Morgan – well known in Wales for his appearances in the Welsh-language soap opera Pobol y Cwm – who voices Luke Skywalker.

In a recent development, “There’s so much excitement about this project and the cast is unbelievable,” Morgan remarked. “I think in Wales we’re on an upward trajectory and this instils a lot of hope. The future is exciting for Wales, particularly in the creative arts. The talent is vast.”.

Sources indicate that asked if he felt the pressure of being Luke Skywalker, he said he was thrilled rather than nervous. “He’s had such an vital impact on my life,” he said. Morgan was also pleased that his 10-year-old brother’s first experience of Star Wars would be in the medium of Welsh. “The fact that Luke tonight in the Welsh language can have that impact on kids here is fantastic.”.

Industry observers note that rhys Ifans, who has appeared in Harry Potter and Spider-Man films, had the tough job of standing in for Alec Guinness as the Jedi master Obi-Wan Kenobi. Sadly, he did not make it to Cardiff for the event.

His brother, Llŷr Ifans, the Welsh voice of the droid C-3PO, was present, however, which was apposite as C-3PO is “fluent in over 6 million forms of communication” – including, clearly, Welsh.

Ifans said: “When I first heard about it, I thought: wow, what are we doing – Star Wars in Welsh? The idea has settled. C-3PO is a genius who speaks over 6 million languages. Now he speaks 6 million and one. He speaks the best language in the world.”.

Asked what accent he used for his C-3PO, Ifans noted: “There are no accents in space. But it’s more about the character. He lives on his nerves and speaks staccato. I had to bring in those aspects.”.

The Welsh-language version of the 1977 film (subsequently retitled Star Wars: Episode IV – A Newly introduced Hope) has been produced by Lucasfilm and Disney in collaboration with the Welsh-language broadcaster S4C and the Welsh government via its Creative Wales agency.

Its Welsh title is Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (Newly introduced Hope). Those not lucky enough to be at the screening in Cardiff will be able to hear the immortal line “May the Force be with you” in Welsh (“A boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi”) when the version is broadcast on S4C platforms on Christmas Day.

Thursday’s screening wasn’t as glitzy as a London or Los Angeles premiere, but it had charm. Côr Bechgyn Glantaf, a schoolboys’ choir from Cardiff, performed as the crowds – including many children – arrived and made their way up the escalators of the multiplex to screens eight and nine. Band Pres Llareggub, which bills itself as a Bronx hip-hop-inspired, New Orleans-tinged brass band with attitude from north Wales, also provided a musical backdrop.

Sources indicate that S4C’s chief executive, Geraint Evans, described the screening as a “hugely proud moment”. He mentioned: “Most importantly, it will give Welsh-speaking children the thrill of hearing some of cinema’s most beloved characters speak their language for the very first time, showing that Welsh can tell any story.”.

There are a few connections linking Wales and Star Wars, not least that a version of the Millennium Falcon was built in south-west Wales.

Mark Williams, who oversaw an exhibition about the Millennium Falcon, remarked he felt the Welsh-language version of the film was long overdue. “I’ve been saying for years it should be done, especially with the ties that Wales has with the franchise,” he said.

Also at the screening was the cabinet minister for enterprise, connectivity and energy in the Welsh government, Adam Price, who mentioned it was an excellent opportunity for Welsh actors and production staff to work with a major Hollywood studio.

“Seeing one of the most iconic films of all time in Welsh is a great way to make the language more accessible and introduces it to new audiences beyond our shores,” he stated.

The Welsh government is aiming to have a million people speaking Cymraeg by 2050. A spokesperson for the Welsh language commissioner’s office said one of its key aims was to increase the use of the language on a community level.

According to recent reports, the spokesperson noted: “In order to do this, the language must be seen and heard in all aspects of our daily lives. The use of Welsh in such a high-profile film as Star Wars has the potential to attract new audiences and raise awareness of the language.”.
