📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here.
  • Recent findings suggest that the 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India.
  • According to recent reports, india has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here.

Recent findings suggest that the 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.

According to recent reports, india has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.

So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.

It has been revealed that my own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.

In a recent development, ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.

‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’.

One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.

Industry observers note that trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.

It has been revealed that the route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.

In a recent development, the following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she stated.

It has been revealed that for Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.

Recent findings suggest that walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.

The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she stated. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.

‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’.

Sources indicate that the travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.

Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.

But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” states Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.

Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.

In a recent development, travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.

Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.

Sources indicate that discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.

Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry remarked that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.

Recent findings suggest that lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.

It has been revealed that culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.

A recommendation from someone with great taste.

Sources indicate that shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”.

Industry observers note that firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board highlighted.

Industry observers note that AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI firm. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.

The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

#47239. This smell startup states its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

This smell startup states its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a lab near Newark Airport in Fresh Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth.
  • “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he notes.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a lab near Newark Airport in Fresh Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”.

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he notes. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It notes its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko notes, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Sources indicate that mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko states. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.).

The firm also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

It has been revealed that osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo introduced, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

In a recent development, but not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn't a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”.

It has been revealed that michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, notes the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

It has been revealed that but even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker states. “Smell is super complex. Context is very crucial for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”.

Sources indicate that in a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

Recent findings suggest that for that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker notes. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”.

This article has been updated with an additional comment from Alex Wiltschko.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Denmark's parliament on Thursday ratified a security agreement with the US over Greenland, hoping to end tensions after US President Donald Trump had repeatedly demanded control over the autonomous Danish territory.

It has been revealed that in the Danish 179-seat parliament, all 109 members present voted in favor of the text. Greenland's parliament already ratified the deal in early November.

US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the ratification, saying in a post on X: "The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO.".

The trilateral security and military access agreement between Washington, Nuuk and Copenhagen allows for expanded US military presence on the mineral-rich and strategically located island in the northern Atlantic.

It also includes permission to establish a "Golden ‌Dome" ​missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

The island is home to some 57,000 people and is strategically located along the shortest route from Europe to North America. It already is home to the northernmost US military base.

The deal was signed in September by Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen but still needed ratification from lawmakers in Greenland and Denmark.

In January 2026, Trump renewed calls for Greenland to become part of the US, threatening military action and tariffs against European allies if they opposed him.

Sources indicate that he argued that Denmark was not able to protect the autonomous Arctic territory from threats by China and Russia. His demands strained US relations with Denmark and alarmed European NATO allies.

Tensions somewhat eased in late January when Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte confirmed a "concept of a deal" that would expand US military access to Greenland. This then led to the agreement being signed in September.

Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has broad military access to Greenland. Denmark had repeatedly said it was open to expanding the US military presence on the island but rejected Trump's demand for full US control.

Tech Report: Dig review: Amy Poehler and Parks and Recs Mike Schur have done it again

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the first time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Parks and Recreation, a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love.
  • Industry observers note that story-wise, the two shows are miles apart.
  • Kicking off that group is Elise (Poehler), the lead archaeologist on a long-running dig in southern Greece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the first time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Parks and Recreation, a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love. The second time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Peacock's upcoming series Dig, which is — you guessed it! — a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love.

Industry observers note that story-wise, the two shows are miles apart. Literally. The former takes place in the decidedly unglamorous town of Pawnee, Indiana, while the latter, based on Kate Myers' novel Excavations, transports us to a sun-bleached archaeological dig in Greece. Yet despite the flashy location and a newly introduced mystery twist, Dig retains the core formula that made Parks and Recreation so irresistible: investing deeply in a lovable new crew of unlikely friends.

Kicking off that group is Elise (Poehler), the lead archaeologist on a long-running dig in southern Greece. She's qualified and passionate, yet has a hard time connecting with the undergraduates (or UGs) participating in the dig. Because of her more guarded exterior, she's consistently second fiddle to longtime dig leader Neville (Hugh Laurie). Perpetually on the brink of retirement, Neville seems unable to cede control of the dig to Elise, both because of his love for archaeology and the ego boost his role gives him. He's the Lucy to Elise's Charlie Brown, constantly yanking the football away at the last second.

So, when Elise discovers a perfectly preserved statue of Hera at an older dig site, the last thing she wants to do is tell Neville and give him an opportunity to claim any shred of credit. However, hiding any cultural artifacts from Neville and the Grecian government at large is illegal, so Elise must assemble a crack team to help her cover up her covert dig of the Hera statue, whom they nickname "Pretty Woman." First up is Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), an always flaky wild card who has unfinished business at the dig. Joining her are Clare (Antonia Thomas), a prim and proper conservator born with a silver spoon in her mouth, and Patty (Fina Strazza), a sheltered farm girl with a deep passion for Greek mythology.

According to recent reports, like with most sitcoms, the characters begin as the broadest versions of themselves before revealing their deeper nuances. At first, Elise is prickly to a fault, allowing Poehler to sidestep any preconceived comparisons you might want to draw to Leslie Knope. Elsewhere, Dylan is the hottest of hot messes, Clare is a haughty queen bee, and Patty is an out-of-her-depth klutz. They border on parodies instead of full-bodied characters, making Dig's earlier episodes a bit lukewarm.

It has been revealed that but as Dig's title suggests, this is a show that won't be satisfied by sticking at surface level. As the show delves into what makes its characters tick, it becomes a heartwarming tale of found family, not unlike many other beloved Schur highlights. Suddenly, character traits that felt one-note to start are revealed to be defense mechanisms or misconceptions, adding entirely fresh dimensions to Dig's core four.

It has been revealed that dig works best when that core works together in earnest, which is another reason why the show's early entries feel like slower burns: They're doing the groundwork to loop every woman into the Pretty Woman dig. Once they're all on the same page, Dig gets off and running — even more so once Pretty Woman mysteriously vanishes, leaving Elise and her motley crew to do some boots-on-the-ground detective work. Thus begins a madcap caper involving stakeouts, undercover identities, and the black market.

Industry observers note that along the way, Elise, Dylan, Clare, and Patty are allowed to be wonderfully messy and vulnerable, all while staying refreshingly supportive of one another. For example, a love triangle burbles up between Clare, Dylan, and Clare's fiancé/Dylan's ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), yet the storyline never devolves into cat fights or possessiveness. Instead, Dig focuses more on what these relationships mean to Clare and Dylan beyond romance. For Clare, her engagement is a sign of stability and true adulthood, whereas Dylan is looking for closure, something she notoriously can never get.

Dig also dabbles in intergenerational conflict, highlighting the differences between each of its leads, all of whom are at very different stages in their lives. Again, Dig doesn't take a hackneyed "Gen Z versus millennials versus Gen X" route. It's more interested in showing the different wants that motivate us. Patty yearns for belonging and friendship, while Elise wants to cement her legacy and make sure she's done something big enough to call her own, no Neville required.

Once Dig's ensemble truly comes together, they mesh wonderfully. Poehler brings a weary exasperation to Elise that slowly gives way to warm leadership, a transformation that's a joy to witness. Thomas and Viswanathan are perfect foils, the former a picture of poise, the latter completely uninhibited. Watching them feed off each other offers up a perfect comedic contrast. Finally, there's Strazza, whose endearingly goofy Patty becomes the beating heart of the show. Laurie, too, is a joy, blending Neville's smarminess with a genial charm that makes him infuriatingly tough to hate.

In a recent development, in focusing on archaeology, Dig emphasizes the importance of excavating ancient objects and interrogating the stories of those who once used them. In many ways, Dig is doing the same thing with its characters: peeling back their layers to get at their core truths. Only instead of using trowels and brushes, Dig uses the power of the workplace sitcom. It's a power Schur and his collaborators know well, and the result is a show that will leave you feeling like you've just uncovered something great in a dig of your own — with far less dirt on your face and clothes, that is.

Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.
  • Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
  • The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes.

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.

The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.

Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.

One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he remarked. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”.

Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.

In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.

Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa noted during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.

After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.

The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that indicated attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

Sources indicate that refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.

During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” noted Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”.

Industry observers note that legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.

The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.

Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.

However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.

The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the ​lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.

Sources indicate that “This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”.

Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already stated Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.

A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.

Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.

The US state department stated in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.

It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and remarked it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.

The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.

Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

#47227. Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents

Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the firm's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire.
  • It has been revealed that “Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks.
  • Sources indicate that the “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the firm's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

It has been revealed that “Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness,” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

Sources indicate that the “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed, so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see; the exploration space that we have to address is huge, and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgment when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”.

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that, in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode-type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” claims Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step; there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated, we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”.

‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world.
  • There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
  • For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world.

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Industry observers note that salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”.

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

According to recent reports, “During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they remarked. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

Industry observers note that “Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”.

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

It has been revealed that she mentioned, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”.

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it noted meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

According to recent reports, “We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” states Salma.

Latest Update: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
  • The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
  • The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.

The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.

The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.

In a recent development, "On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.

He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ICJ stated in its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.

Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa mentioned.

"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa mentioned.

Iwasawa also stated that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.

At one point, reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested.".

He noted this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.

There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military, which is regarded as the real underlying power.

Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.

Recent findings suggest that "The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has.".

Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering.".

And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Rohingya people, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home.".

Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.

It noted that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide.".

Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities, but the extent to which Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.

"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families.".

Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterward at the Peace Palace in The Hague.

"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe.".

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment.".

According to recent reports, miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya.".

UN human rights chief Volker Türk noted the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind.".

The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.

Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.

It has been revealed that A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.

Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.

Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect.".

The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person noted, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person noted, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical newly introduced insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have noted.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it states is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

Sources indicate that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official mentioned in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

According to recent reports, gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, noted at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

It has been revealed that the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

It has been revealed that still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

In a recent development, tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

It has been revealed that “It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”.

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”.

Jensen Huang has visited this shaved ice stall at Taipei’s Linjiang Street Night Market three times since 2023.

It has been revealed that tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.

Sources indicate that “When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”.

At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Tech giant (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.

Industry observers note that “I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh stated of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”.

Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, remarked that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.

Owner Tu Chang-chun noted he has no plans to take down photos Jensen Huang visiting his shaved-ice shop.

In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion Fresh Taiwan dollars.

The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.

Sources indicate that but not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business.

The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.

Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”.

Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”.

A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.

Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.

Sources indicate that suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.

Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.

He mentioned he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.

But Todd Blanche, the United States attorney general, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Trump.

“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” Blanche said after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.

“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”.

US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.

Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.

#47214. What a billion-dollar deal states about the US battery market

What a billion-dollar deal states about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • Recent findings suggest that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila states could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

Recent findings suggest that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

In a recent development, founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the tech giant. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the manufacturer when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Recent findings suggest that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced looks for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

Sources indicate that the tech giant opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky indicates, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a significant one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

APEC summit: Trump, Xi, Putin talks end with 'peace declaration'
